title: A Differential Drive That Slips: Wheel Speeds to Motion, With the Two Losses a Real Floor Adds, and What Each Costs in Distance and in Turn

questions.question: Which loss takes a fraction of every turn?
options: The step size of the integration
questions.explanation: Slip shortens the distance travelled, which on a straight line is only a scale error. Turn efficiency shortens every turn, and a short turn misdirects everything after it.

questions.question: 10 m of wheel travel with 5 percent slip was how far on the ground?
options: 10.00 m: slip only matters in turns
questions.explanation: The ground distance is the wheel travel times one less the slip: 10 m times 0.95.

questions.question: A turn the wheels say is 90 degrees, at an efficiency of 0.8, was:
questions.explanation: The body's turn is the efficiency times what the wheel difference says: 0.8 of 90 degrees.

questions.question: How much more wheel travel does a turn need at efficiency 0.8?
questions.explanation: To get the full turn the wheels must ask for one over 0.8 of it, which is a quarter more.

questions.question: Why does the square not close?
options: The slip shortens each side by a different amount
The integration uses the heading at the start of the step
The wheels are of different sizes
Each turn is short, so the next side points the wrong way, and the error grows with the side
questions.explanation: With turns 10 percent short the second side is already misdirected, and the miss grows with the side's length. With 2 percent slip and 0.9 efficiency it ended 4.64 m from home.

questions.question: How can the efficiency be found?
options: From the tyre maker's data sheet
By driving a straight line and timing it
From a measured turn: the body's turn over the turn the wheels ask for
questions.explanation: It depends on floor, tyres and weight, so it has to be measured. A turn made with an efficiency of 0.8 read back as 0.800.
